source: LS5009 · Dr Hossein Ashrafi · Cellular Injury III · 2026 student notes · 30 slides

cards.text: When injury exceeds a cell’s capacity to adapt and recover, it becomes {{c1::irreversible}} and can lead to cell death.
cards.question: When injury exceeds a cell’s capacity to adapt and recover, it becomes {{c1::irreversible}} and can lead to cell death.

cards.text: Adaptation establishes a {{c1::new steady state}}; irreversible injury leads to cell death rather than successful adaptation.
cards.question: Adaptation establishes a {{c1::new steady state}}; irreversible injury leads to cell death rather than successful adaptation.

cards.text: The two cell-death patterns emphasised in this lecture are {{c1::necrosis}} and {{c2::apoptosis}}.
cards.question: The two cell-death patterns emphasised in this lecture are {{c1::necrosis}} and {{c2::apoptosis}}.

cards.text: The two cell-death patterns emphasised in this lecture are {{c1::necrosis}} and {{c2::apoptosis}}.
cards.question: The two cell-death patterns emphasised in this lecture are {{c1::necrosis}} and {{c2::apoptosis}}.

cards.text: Necrosis and apoptosis differ in morphology, mechanisms and their roles in {{c1::physiology and disease}}.
cards.question: Necrosis and apoptosis differ in morphology, mechanisms and their roles in {{c1::physiology and disease}}.

cards.text: Apoptosis is an organised cellular death programme that can be triggered by {{c1::internal or external signals}}.
cards.question: Apoptosis is an organised cellular death programme that can be triggered by {{c1::internal or external signals}}.

cards.text: Mechanical injury and toxic chemicals can cause cell death with a {{c1::necrotic}} pattern.
cards.question: Mechanical injury and toxic chemicals can cause cell death with a {{c1::necrotic}} pattern.

cards.text: Necrosis describes the morphological changes of dead cells within {{c1::living tissue}}.
cards.question: Necrosis describes the morphological changes of dead cells within {{c1::living tissue}}.

cards.text: Necrosis is a {{c1::pathological}} process, unlike physiological removal of cells during normal development.
cards.question: Necrosis is a {{c1::pathological}} process, unlike physiological removal of cells during normal development.

cards.text: Hypoxia, ischaemia, infection, toxins and mechanical damage can cause {{c1::necrosis}}.
cards.question: Hypoxia, ischaemia, infection, toxins and mechanical damage can cause {{c1::necrosis}}.

cards.text: Can a necrotic cell resume normal integrated function? {{c1::No—the cell-death changes are irreversible}}.
cards.question: Can a necrotic cell resume normal integrated function? {{c1::No—the cell-death changes are irreversible}}.

cards.text: Necrotic cells typically {{c1::swell}} before membrane disruption and lysis.
cards.question: Necrotic cells typically {{c1::swell}} before membrane disruption and lysis.

cards.text: A central feature of necrosis is loss of {{c1::plasma-membrane integrity}}.
cards.question: A central feature of necrosis is loss of {{c1::plasma-membrane integrity}}.

cards.text: When the plasma membrane ruptures, cellular contents {{c1::leak into surrounding tissue}}.
cards.question: When the plasma membrane ruptures, cellular contents {{c1::leak into surrounding tissue}}.

cards.text: Leakage from necrotic cells can injure neighbours and stimulate {{c1::inflammation}}.
cards.question: Leakage from necrotic cells can injure neighbours and stimulate {{c1::inflammation}}.

cards.text: Severe lysosomal membrane damage releases {{c1::digestive enzymes}} into the cytoplasm.
cards.question: Severe lysosomal membrane damage releases {{c1::digestive enzymes}} into the cytoplasm.

cards.text: Enzymatic breakdown of a dead cell contributes to {{c1::cell lysis}}.
cards.question: Enzymatic breakdown of a dead cell contributes to {{c1::cell lysis}}.

cards.text: Mitochondrial swelling and rupture are features of the lecture’s {{c1::necrotic-cell}} sequence.
cards.question: Mitochondrial swelling and rupture are features of the lecture’s {{c1::necrotic-cell}} sequence.

cards.text: Why is necrosis commonly inflammatory? {{c1::Membrane rupture releases intracellular material into the surrounding tissue}}.
cards.question: Why is necrosis commonly inflammatory? {{c1::Membrane rupture releases intracellular material into the surrounding tissue}}.
cards.answer: Membrane rupture releases intracellular material into the surrounding tissue

cards.text: In an infarct, necrotic tissue lies beside {{c1::surviving tissue}}, allowing comparison of their morphology.
cards.question: In an infarct, necrotic tissue lies beside {{c1::surviving tissue}}, allowing comparison of their morphology.

cards.text: Coagulative, liquefactive, caseous and fat necrosis describe different {{c1::tissue patterns}} of necrosis.
cards.question: Coagulative, liquefactive, caseous and fat necrosis describe different {{c1::tissue patterns}} of necrosis.

cards.text: The pattern of necrosis depends partly on the {{c1::tissue and type of injury}}, rather than all dead tissues looking identical.
cards.question: The pattern of necrosis depends partly on the {{c1::tissue and type of injury}}, rather than all dead tissues looking identical.

cards.text: In coagulative necrosis, recognisable {{c1::cell outlines and tissue architecture}} are initially preserved.
cards.question: In coagulative necrosis, recognisable {{c1::cell outlines and tissue architecture}} are initially preserved.

cards.text: Coagulative necrotic tissue is often relatively {{c1::firm}}.
cards.question: Coagulative necrotic tissue is often relatively {{c1::firm}}.

cards.text: Renal infarction is a classic example of {{c1::coagulative necrosis}}.
cards.question: Renal infarction is a classic example of {{c1::coagulative necrosis}}.

cards.text: Denaturation of structural proteins and enzymes slows {{c1::proteolytic digestion}}, helping preserve dead-cell outlines.
cards.question: Denaturation of structural proteins and enzymes slows {{c1::proteolytic digestion}}, helping preserve dead-cell outlines.

cards.text: Coagulative necrotic debris is eventually removed by {{c1::phagocytosis}}.
cards.question: Coagulative necrotic debris is eventually removed by {{c1::phagocytosis}}.

cards.text: A kidney infarct retains ghost-like cell outlines. The expected pattern is {{c1::coagulative necrosis}}.
cards.question: A kidney infarct retains ghost-like cell outlines. The expected pattern is {{c1::coagulative necrosis}}.

cards.text: In the lecture’s renal-infarct micrograph, N labels normal kidney and I labels the {{c1::infarcted tissue}}.
cards.question: In the lecture’s renal-infarct micrograph, N labels normal kidney and I labels the {{c1::infarcted tissue}}.

cards.text: Preserved architecture does not mean preserved viability: cells with retained outlines can still be {{c1::dead}}.
cards.question: Preserved architecture does not mean preserved viability: cells with retained outlines can still be {{c1::dead}}.

cards.text: In liquefactive necrosis, enzymatic digestion turns dead tissue into a {{c1::soft or liquid mass}}.
cards.question: In liquefactive necrosis, enzymatic digestion turns dead tissue into a {{c1::soft or liquid mass}}.

cards.text: A brain infarct classically undergoes {{c1::liquefactive necrosis}}.
cards.question: A brain infarct classically undergoes {{c1::liquefactive necrosis}}.

cards.text: Liquefactive necrosis removes recognisable architecture through {{c1::digestion of dead cells}}.
cards.question: Liquefactive necrosis removes recognisable architecture through {{c1::digestion of dead cells}}.

cards.text: A renal infarct is typically coagulative; a cerebral infarct is typically {{c1::liquefactive}}.
cards.question: A renal infarct is typically coagulative; a cerebral infarct is typically {{c1::liquefactive}}.

cards.text: An ischaemic brain lesion dissolves rather than retaining firm cell outlines. This illustrates {{c1::liquefactive necrosis}}.
cards.question: An ischaemic brain lesion dissolves rather than retaining firm cell outlines. This illustrates {{c1::liquefactive necrosis}}.

cards.text: Caseous necrosis has a characteristic {{c1::cheese-like}} gross appearance.
cards.question: Caseous necrosis has a characteristic {{c1::cheese-like}} gross appearance.
cards.explanation: Caseous necrosis loses architecture; classic coagulative necrosis initially preserves it.

cards.text: Tuberculosis lesions are a classic setting for {{c1::caseous necrosis}}.
cards.question: Tuberculosis lesions are a classic setting for {{c1::caseous necrosis}}.

cards.text: The lecture’s tuberculous lung contains {{c1::yellow-white, cheesy debris}}.
cards.question: The lecture’s tuberculous lung contains {{c1::yellow-white, cheesy debris}}.

cards.text: Does caseous necrosis preserve recognisable architecture like classic coagulative necrosis? {{c1::No—caseous tissue is disrupted into amorphous necrotic debris}}.
cards.question: Does caseous necrosis preserve recognisable architecture like classic coagulative necrosis? {{c1::No—caseous tissue is disrupted into amorphous necrotic debris}}.

cards.text: The lecture’s bovine-bronchus specimen demonstrates {{c1::caseous necrosis}}.
cards.question: The lecture’s bovine-bronchus specimen demonstrates {{c1::caseous necrosis}}.

cards.text: Enzymatic fat necrosis is especially associated with release of {{c1::pancreatic lipases}}.
cards.question: Enzymatic fat necrosis is especially associated with release of {{c1::pancreatic lipases}}.

cards.text: Lipases split neutral fat into {{c1::glycerol}} and {{c2::fatty acids}}.
cards.question: Lipases split neutral fat into {{c1::glycerol}} and {{c2::fatty acids}}.

cards.text: Lipases split neutral fat into {{c1::glycerol}} and {{c2::fatty acids}}.
cards.question: Lipases split neutral fat into {{c1::glycerol}} and {{c2::fatty acids}}.

cards.text: Released fatty acids can combine with {{c1::calcium}} to form insoluble soaps.
cards.question: Released fatty acids can combine with {{c1::calcium}} to form insoluble soaps.

cards.text: Calcium-soap formation following fat breakdown is called {{c1::saponification}}.
cards.question: Calcium-soap formation following fat breakdown is called {{c1::saponification}}.

cards.text: Chalky white deposits in damaged fatty tissue can represent {{c1::fat necrosis with saponification}}.
cards.question: Chalky white deposits in damaged fatty tissue can represent {{c1::fat necrosis with saponification}}.

cards.text: Pancreatic injury releases digestive enzymes into surrounding fat. The expected local pattern is {{c1::enzymatic fat necrosis}}.
cards.question: Pancreatic injury releases digestive enzymes into surrounding fat. The expected local pattern is {{c1::enzymatic fat necrosis}}.

cards.text: The white deposits of fat necrosis are chemically related to {{c1::calcium salts of fatty acids}}, not simply intact stored fat.
cards.question: The white deposits of fat necrosis are chemically related to {{c1::calcium salts of fatty acids}}, not simply intact stored fat.

cards.text: Fat necrosis can occur in adipose tissue at sites outside the pancreas; the lecture shows {{c1::perirenal fat}} in a cow.
cards.question: Fat necrosis can occur in adipose tissue at sites outside the pancreas; the lecture shows {{c1::perirenal fat}} in a cow.

cards.text: Gangrene is a clinical term often used for extensive {{c1::ischaemic necrosis}} of a limb.
cards.question: Gangrene is a clinical term often used for extensive {{c1::ischaemic necrosis}} of a limb.
cards.explanation: Dry gangrene need not be infected; wet gangrene has superimposed infection.

cards.text: The distal foot and toes in a person with diabetes are a typical setting for {{c1::gangrene}}.
cards.question: The distal foot and toes in a person with diabetes are a typical setting for {{c1::gangrene}}.

cards.text: Dry gangrene is predominantly ischaemic; wet gangrene includes {{c1::superimposed infection}}.
cards.question: Dry gangrene is predominantly ischaemic; wet gangrene includes {{c1::superimposed infection}}.

cards.text: Is infection required for every case of gangrene? {{c1::No—dry gangrene can occur without infection}}.
cards.question: Is infection required for every case of gangrene? {{c1::No—dry gangrene can occur without infection}}.
cards.answer: No—dry gangrene can occur without infection

cards.text: Impaired blood supply causes gangrenous necrosis by depriving tissue of {{c1::oxygen and nutrients}}.
cards.question: Impaired blood supply causes gangrenous necrosis by depriving tissue of {{c1::oxygen and nutrients}}.

cards.text: Apoptosis can be initiated by signals originating inside the cell or from {{c1::outside the cell}}.
cards.question: Apoptosis can be initiated by signals originating inside the cell or from {{c1::outside the cell}}.

cards.text: Apoptosis commonly removes {{c1::individual cells or small groups of cells}} while neighbouring tissue remains functional.
cards.question: Apoptosis commonly removes {{c1::individual cells or small groups of cells}} while neighbouring tissue remains functional.
cards.answer: individual cells or small groups of cells

cards.text: Apoptosis is a regulated process under cellular control, rather than simple {{c1::rupture from overwhelming damage}}.
cards.question: Apoptosis is a regulated process under cellular control, rather than simple {{c1::rupture from overwhelming damage}}.

cards.text: The term apoptosis originally refers to {{c1::leaves falling from a tree}}.
cards.question: The term apoptosis originally refers to {{c1::leaves falling from a tree}}.

cards.text: Removal of cells between developing digits helps form separate {{c1::fingers and toes}}.
cards.question: Removal of cells between developing digits helps form separate {{c1::fingers and toes}}.

cards.text: Resorption of the tadpole tail is a developmental example of {{c1::apoptosis}}.
cards.question: Resorption of the tadpole tail is a developmental example of {{c1::apoptosis}}.

cards.text: Apoptosis contributes to normal tissue turnover, including cyclical changes in the {{c1::uterine lining}}.
cards.question: Apoptosis contributes to normal tissue turnover, including cyclical changes in the {{c1::uterine lining}}.

cards.text: Virus-infected cells, cells with severe DNA damage and abnormal cells may be eliminated by {{c1::apoptosis}}.
cards.question: Virus-infected cells, cells with severe DNA damage and abnormal cells may be eliminated by {{c1::apoptosis}}.

cards.text: Apoptosis contributes to development as well as {{c1::removal of potentially harmful cells}}.
cards.question: Apoptosis contributes to development as well as {{c1::removal of potentially harmful cells}}.

cards.text: The DNA-damage response described in the lecture involves the tumour-suppressor protein {{c1::p53}}.
cards.question: The DNA-damage response described in the lecture involves the tumour-suppressor protein {{c1::p53}}.

cards.text: p53 can help coordinate repair responses; if damage cannot be resolved, it can promote {{c1::apoptosis}}.
cards.question: p53 can help coordinate repair responses; if damage cannot be resolved, it can promote {{c1::apoptosis}}.

cards.text: Apoptotic removal of a cell with irreparable DNA damage prevents survival of a potentially {{c1::genetically abnormal cell}}.
cards.question: Apoptotic removal of a cell with irreparable DNA damage prevents survival of a potentially {{c1::genetically abnormal cell}}.

cards.text: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes can trigger apoptosis in {{c1::virus-infected cells}}.
cards.question: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes can trigger apoptosis in {{c1::virus-infected cells}}.

cards.text: Does every DNA-damage signal automatically lead to apoptosis? {{c1::No—the cell may first repair the damage; death depends on the damage and response}}.
cards.question: Does every DNA-damage signal automatically lead to apoptosis? {{c1::No—the cell may first repair the damage; death depends on the damage and response}}.
cards.answer: No—the cell may first repair the damage; death depends on the damage and response

cards.text: Deficient apoptosis can allow abnormal cells to survive and contribute to {{c1::cancer}}.
cards.question: Deficient apoptosis can allow abnormal cells to survive and contribute to {{c1::cancer}}.

cards.text: Loss of normal p53 function can weaken elimination of cells with {{c1::damaged DNA}}.
cards.question: Loss of normal p53 function can weaken elimination of cells with {{c1::damaged DNA}}.

cards.question: Some viruses interfere with p53-dependent responses, helping infected cells {{c1::evade elimination}}.

cards.question: The high-risk HPV type used as an example in the lecture is {{c1::HPV16}}.

cards.question: Failure to remove a damaged cell can promote cancer; excessive removal of needed cells can cause {{c1::tissue loss}}.

cards.text: Excessive apoptosis can contribute to pathological {{c1::loss of functional cells}}.
cards.question: Excessive apoptosis can contribute to pathological {{c1::loss of functional cells}}.

to the pancreas. Lipases released from the pancreas split the neutral fat 
in lipid cells into glycerol and fatty acids, which diffuse out of the cells.

Apoptosis
• In pathology used to describe specific type of cell

• Involves death of individual cells or small groups

• From Greek:

slides.topic: Why should a cell commit suicide?
slides.text:
Why should a cell commit suicide?
➢Apoptosis is needed for proper development
 
–The resorption of the tadpole tail  
–The formation of the fingers and toes of the fetus 
–The sloughing off of the inner lining of the uterus
➢Apoptosis is needed to destroy cells 
 
 
–Cells infected with viruses 
–Cells with DNA damage 
–Cancer cells
Importance of Apoptosis

Apoptosis
➢Apoptosis is needed to destroy cells that represent a 
threat to the integrity of the organism
– Cells with damaged DNA 
DNA damage activates a protein called p53 which can facilitate DNA repair.  If 
this is not successful the p53 system can then induce apoptosis and so 
eliminate the damaged cells.  
– Cells infected with viruses
elimination of viral infected cells by T lymphocytes

Apoptosis and disease
1. Deficient apoptosis
– Cancers
Dysfunction of Tumor suppressor gene (p53)
– Viral Infections
Some viruses can degrade p53 function
E.g. Human Papillomavirus type 16 causative agent of Cervical 
Cancer

2. Excess apoptosis
Neurodegenerative diseases
– Alzheimers Disease
– Parkinsons Disease

editorialNotes: The deck follows the scope of this introductory lecture; necrosis and apoptosis are not an exhaustive list of modern cell-death mechanisms. Necrotic death can also be regulated.

Slide 29 is simplified: apoptosis occurs in physiological and pathological settings; necrosis can show nuclear shrinkage, fragmentation and dissolution. Apoptosis usually elicits little inflammation when apoptotic bodies are cleared promptly.
Caseous necrosis is taught as a distinct cheese-like pattern with loss of recognisable architecture, rather than equating it with preserved-architecture coagulative necrosis.
Gangrene is a clinical description. Dry gangrene can be ischaemic without infection; wet gangrene involves superimposed infection. Infection is not required for all gangrene.

The lecture’s apoptosis signalling flowchart is schematic, not a universal sequence in which new death-gene transcription is always necessary. Membrane blebbing is distinguished from early membrane rupture.

p53 helps coordinate responses to DNA damage; it can support repair or promote apoptosis if damage cannot be resolved. Neurodegenerative diseases are multifactorial, so excess apoptosis is not presented as their sole cause.

Visual prompts use lecture figure crops with answer headings excluded. Images illustrate the source examples and are not presented as independently diagnostic. Full original source slides remain available.
